questions.q: Why do we need to separate the components of a mixture? Give examples.
answer: A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically combined, and we often need to separate them.

answer.text: We separate out harmful or useless material — for example, picking stones out of rice, or removing husk from grain.
We separate to collect something valuable — for example, getting salt from seawater, or cream from milk.
The method depends on the properties of the components — their size, weight, magnetism or solubility. Thus different situations call for handpicking, winnowing, filtration, evaporation and so on.

questions.q: Describe the common methods used to separate solids from liquids.
answer: Several methods separate solids from liquids, depending on whether the solid is soluble.

answer.text: A heavier insoluble solid is allowed to settle at the bottom as sediment; the clear liquid above is then carefully poured off, which is decantation.
The mixture is passed through a filter, which holds back insoluble solids while the liquid passes through — used to remove tea leaves or to separate sand from water.
To recover a soluble solid, the liquid is evaporated by heating, leaving the solid behind — this is how salt is obtained from seawater.

questions.q: What is a saturated solution, and how can more solute be made to dissolve?
answer: When a soluble solid dissolves evenly in a liquid, the result is a solution, in which the liquid is the solvent.

answer.text: As more and more solute is added, a point is reached where no more will dissolve at that temperature. Such a solution is said to be saturated.
Heating the solution usually allows more solute to dissolve, because solubility increases with temperature. On cooling or on evaporating the solvent, the extra solute separates out again.

answer: This is why warm water dissolves more sugar or salt than cold water.
